analysis.one_liner: Makes it an unfair labor practice for employers to permanently replace striking workers.
analysis.headline: After clearing a Senate committee, the bill never reached the floor: two cloture votes failed 53-47 and 53-46, seven short of the 60 needed to proceed.
analysis.plain_summary: Under long-standing labor law, an employer can hire permanent replacements for workers on strike, and those workers lose their jobs even if the strike was lawful. This bill would make that an unfair labor practice: employers could use temporary replacements during a dispute, but would have to take striking workers back and could not favor replacements over returning strikers for other jobs. It would apply the same rule to railroads and airlines under the Railway Labor Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who strike or engage in other collective action. They would keep the right to return to their jobs after a lawful strike, instead of being permanently replaced, and would keep their seniority and other job rights when they return.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to hire, promise, or threaten to hire a permanent replacement for a worker engaged in a lawful labor dispute in a unionized bargaining unit [S2][S3].
Bars employers from denying returning strikers their other job rights or privileges out of preference for replacement workers who crossed the picket line [S2][S3].
Applies the same protections to railroad and airline employees by amending the Railway Labor Act [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing strikes, especially in manufacturing, transportation, and other unionized industries, who would lose permanent replacement as a way to keep operating and to pressure strikers to settle. They could still use temporary replacements but could not dismiss the strikers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers who use permanent striker replacements

drawbacks.text: Employers and their allies argued that companies must be able to keep operating during a strike, and that banning permanent replacements would give unions leverage to win higher settlements, with costs passed on in prices or relocations. Six Senate Democrats joined nearly all Republicans in voting to block the bill [S6][S7].

The bill's protection is limited: it covers employees who were in a unionized bargaining unit, or a unit seeking certification on written authorization from a majority of employees, so workers outside that structure get no new protection [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers in unionized workplaces, the bill would have removed the single biggest financial risk of striking — losing the job permanently. The cost falls on employers in strike-prone industries, who lose a potent bargaining weapon, with some possible spillover into prices and where companies choose to operate. That tradeoff was exactly what the Senate refused to even debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared committee but opponents never allowed debate to start: two cloture votes on the motion to proceed failed at 53-47 and 53-46, well short of the 60 needed, and the motion was then withdrawn.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Metzenbaum with 40 cosponsors and reported favorably without amendment by the Labor and Human Resources Committee in July 1993, then placed on the Senate calendar [S5].
When supporters tried to bring it to the floor in July 1994, a first cloture vote on the motion to proceed failed 53-47, with Democrats voting 50-6 in favor and Republicans 3-41 [S6].

A second cloture attempt the next day also failed, 53-46, with the same partisan split, and the motion to proceed was then withdrawn, leaving the bill unconsidered for the rest of the Congress [S7][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in unionized industries keep the right to permanently replace striking workers, and the organized opposition that blocked the bill kept it off the floor without a single up-or-down vote on its merits.

sides.party_line_note: Cloture failed 53-47 and 53-46: 50 of 56 Democrats voted yes while 3 of 44 Republicans did, and six Democrats crossed over to the opposition both times.

industries.note: The bill would take away permanent replacement as a strike-management tool, costing employers leverage in labor disputes but restoring job security for striking workers. Its interest here runs against the workers it would protect.
The ban would make striking far less risky, strengthening unions' ability to bargain and to organize new units, since workers could not be permanently replaced for exercising that right.
Carriers covered by the Railway Labor Act would face the same ban on permanent replacements during disputes, losing a tool they have used in past national strikes.
